children: Social Security is on the ballot this fall, even though it has taken a back seat to the economy and other concerns on the campaign trail.

In the midterm elections, voters will elect the first class of senators who will be in office during the projected depletion date of the retirement trust fund in 2032. They will have no choice but to confront the funding shortfall that politicians have punted for decades.

If Congress fails to act, beneficiaries face an automatic cut benefit of 26%, according to Congressional Budget Office projections in September. The Social Security Trustees projected a lower but still devastating cut of 22% in their June report. At that point, incoming payroll taxes would continue to fund the bulk of benefits, but the trust fund — a financial cushion that currently makes up the difference between what Social Security pays out in benefits and what it collects in revenue — will have run dry.
"Something's got to happen," says Max Richtman, president and CEO of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.
The status quo won't protect benefits, and voters should press congressional candidates on their plans to shore up the program, Richtman says. "'I'm for Social Security' isn't enough," he says.

Many predict Congress will wait until the depletion deadline nears and then pass some combination of tax increases and benefit cuts for future recipients. Typically, Democrats are more in favor of raising revenue than Republicans, yet it's too early to say how the composition of Congress may affect the balance of fixes that lawmakers adopt, says Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist for Stifel. A third of the Senate is up for reelection every two years for a six-year term, the entire U.S. House of Representatives is up for re-election every two years, and the White House will change hands in 2029.

On Capitol Hill, Social Security is gaining traction, Gardner says: "People are starting to discuss it with a greater sense of urgency." Yet the issue still isn't top of mind, he says, and talk on the campaign trail is mostly "platitudes."

One candidate who has come out in favor of a fix is Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate from Maine. He has called for "scrapping the cap," the Social Security payroll tax that funds benefits. Under current law, the 12.4% tax is split equally between employers and workers and is levied on incomes up to $184,500 in 2026, rising to $192,300 next year. Lifting it completely would close about 60% of the program's funding shortfall, assuming higher earners are given no benefit credit for their additional contribution.

This proposal has garnered rare bipartisan support. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) and Sen. Bernie Moreno (R., Ohio) are working on legislation that would eliminate the payroll-tax cap, the two wrote in a New York Times opinion piece this summer. Moreno's support for the measure is "huge," Richtman says.

Whatever Congress does, it's unlikely that current Social Security recipients and those within at least a decade of retirement will face any changes to their benefit amount. In 1983, the last time Congress undertook large-scale Social Security reform, lawmakers changed the benefit calculation for everyone ages 45 and under at the time. The provision very gradually raised the age for full benefits to 67 from 65, a de facto benefit cut.

The 1983 changes also imposed income taxes on partial Social Security benefits. It's possible that lawmakers could again change the way benefits are taxed, or even broaden the tax base to include investment income — similar to the 3.8% net investment income tax that since 2013 has been imposed on higher-income taxpayers.

Some Republicans are saying on the stump that the One Big Beautiful Bill got rid of Social Security taxes. However, the 2025 law didn't change the rules on Social Security taxation. Instead, it created a temporary $6,000 senior deduction that in effect eliminated Social Security taxes for many qualifying middle-income recipients. The deduction is set to sunset in 2029.
